title: Women in the teaching
hook: the Gurus honored women as equals, as teachers and as leaders

segments.voice: Yesterday, the langar row: one strip of cloth, one ladle, the same light in everyone. Your line was equal souls. Whom did you stop ranking, even for a minute? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-three.

Why call her bad? That's the question, and it comes from Guru Nanak, in the middle of a long hymn. Around him, a woman could be treated as a lesser thing: unclean at certain times, blamed for misfortune, expected in some places to follow her husband into the fire when he died. Guru Nanak doesn't start with a rule. He starts with the plain facts of a life. Who carries the child? Who is a man engaged to, married to, befriended by? Who keeps the family going when someone dies? And then the question lands: why call her bad, from whom kings are born? Yesterday was equal souls. Today, the half of humanity that question was for.
screen: `WHY CALL HER BAD?` → `THE PLAIN FACTS OF A LIFE.` → `FROM WHOM KINGS ARE BORN.`

segments.voice: First, the hymn. It sits in Asa di Var, the morning hymn sung in gurdwaras. In paraphrase: from woman we are born, in woman we are conceived, to woman we are engaged and married; through woman the generations go on. So why call her bad, from whom kings are born? It's an argument from the kitchen table, not from a throne. Second, a woman at the hearth. The Granth keeps a hymn by the bards Balwand and Satta, and in it they praise Mata Khivi, the wife of Guru Angad. In paraphrase: Khivi was good, her shade was cool and leafy, and she gave out rich sweet rice to all. Tradition remembers her as the one who ran the Guru's langar. The community kitchen, the floor where yesterday's equality became dinner, had a woman at its center. Third, a custom refused. Guru Amar Das speaks against the burning of widows. In paraphrase from a salok: those who burn with their husband's body are not truly sati; the true ones are those who live on in love and goodness. Tradition also says he appointed women among the teachers he sent out to guide the sangat. Fourth, leaders. Sikh memory holds Mata Gujri, mother of Guru Gobind Singh, steady through the hardest days, and Mai Bhago, who tradition says rallied men who had turned back and rode out with them. Teachers, cooks, mothers, leaders. And it's honest to add: the teaching is clear, and living up to it in every gurdwara and family is still a work in progress. The words remain: equals.
screen: `ASA DI VAR: WHY CALL HER BAD?` · `MATA KHIVI AT THE LANGAR.` · `GURU AMAR DAS REFUSES THE PYRE.` · `MATA GUJRI, MAI BHAGO.` · then, large: `EQUALS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to a woman's teaching. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a woman who taught you something real: a grandmother, a teacher, a neighbor, a boss, a friend. Hear one thing she said, in her own voice. Breathe in with it. Breathe out and let it land again, as if for the first time. If nobody comes to mind, plan to listen today, fully, to a woman's words, a talk, a book, a conversation, without waiting for your turn to speak. The bell holds the time.
Women in the teaching. The Gurus honored women as equals: Guru Nanak's why call her bad, Mata Khivi at the langar, and Guru Amar Das refusing the widow's pyre. Today's word.
Your line: equals. Today, in one meeting or one meal, notice whose voice gets interrupted, and make room for it to finish. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-three.

screen: `DAY 1383 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FORCE AS THE LAST RESORT.`

howItsDone: In gurdwaras women and men can lead kirtan, read from the Guru Granth Sahib and serve in the langar; Sikhs remember women such as Mata Khivi, Mata Gujri and Mai Bhago.

fork.setup: you're Guru Amar Das, and the custom says a widow should follow her husband into the fire. what do you say?
options: praise her courage, as the custom does.
stay silent; it's a family matter.
say the true sati lives on in love and goodness.
fork.reveal: his salok says those who burn with the body are not truly sati; living on in love is the true way.

trapdoor: what you thought: old scriptures keep women in the background.
what it means: the Gurus spoke of women as equals and honored them as teachers and leaders.
what a scholar hears: the Granth itself names Mata Khivi, in the hymn of the bards Balwand and Satta.
